claims.text: The target lightweight Mg-containing high-entropy alloy initially has a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-containing microstructure.
Thermal annealing conditions can modulate phase decomposition or precipitation behavior in the target alloy.
Exposure at roughly 850–1050 °C for sufficient time promotes measurable elemental diffusion in the target alloy.
Thermal activation enhances local Mg diffusion.
Mg diffusion produces local compositional fluctuations that cause Mg-rich intermetallic compounds to nucleate and grow.
Mg-rich intermetallic compounds preferentially segregate or form at grain boundaries.
Prolonged annealing above a critical time-temperature threshold produces a coarser intermetallic distribution than rapid quenching.
Coarsened or segregated Mg-rich intermetallics disrupt the continuity and chemical homogeneity of protective high-temperature oxide scales.
Coarsened or segregated Mg-rich intermetallics reduce oxide-scale adherence.
Disruption of protective oxide scales reduces high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the initial metastable state.
Formation of Mg-rich intermetallics reduces corrosion resistance relative to the initial metastable state.
The as-quenched metastable solid-solution state forms continuous, adherent high-temperature oxide scales that provide good oxidation and corrosion resistance.
Keeping thermal exposure below a critical kinetic threshold limits intermetallic formation.
Kinetically limiting intermetallic growth preserves a more uniform solid solution and protective behavior.
A critical combination of temperature and exposure time exists at which Mg-driven precipitation becomes sufficient to impair oxide-scale performance.
